key_terms.meaning: Separate program (code) memory and data memory, each with its own bus, so code and data can be fetched at the same time
8-bit SFR at address D0H holding CY, AC, F0, RS1, RS0, OV, and P (parity) flags
One of the 128 on-chip registers at addresses 80H–FFH that control ports, timers, serial port and interrupts
16-bit data pointer formed by SFR pair DPH (83H) and DPL (82H), used for external and table memory access
Pin 30; pulses high to latch the low byte of an external address from P0 during external memory access
A port pin with a weak internal pull-up and a strong pull-down, so it can sink current but must be written 1 to be read as an input
An instruction such as INC P1 or ANL P1,A that reads the port latch (not the pin), changes it, and writes it back
12 oscillator periods in the standard 8051; one timer count equals one machine cycle
8-bit SFR at 89H; low nibble sets Timer 0 and high nibble sets Timer 1 as timer or counter and selects mode 0–3
Two separate registers at 99H: one for the byte to transmit, one for the byte received; reading and writing give different bytes
8-bit SFR at 98H holding SM0, SM1, SM2, REN, TB8, RB8, TI and RI for serial mode and control
Symbols per second on the serial line; in 8051 mode 1 it equals (2^SMOD ÷ 32) × (Timer 1 overflow rate)
Interface IC that converts 8051 TTL levels (0 V / 5 V) to RS-232 levels (about +10 V / −10 V) and back
Fixed code address where the CPU jumps for a source: 0003H (INT0), 000BH (Timer 0), 0013H (INT1), 001BH (Timer 1), 0023H (serial)
SFR at A8H with bits EA, ES, ET1, EX1, ET0 and EX0; EA must be 1 for any interrupt to reach the CPU
SFR at B8H; a 1 in a bit makes that source high priority, which can interrupt a low-priority service routine
Keil C51 keyword that names one bit of an SFR, e.g. sbit LED = P1^0;
C qualifier telling the compiler a variable can change outside program flow, so it must not be cached in a register
PIC18F452 scheme where an 8-bit BSR (or the BSF/BCF access bit) selects which 256-byte bank of data memory is visible
MSP430 sleep state (LPM0–LPM4) that stops the CPU clock and selected clocks; LPM4 keeps only RAM and wakes on an interrupt

takeaways: The 8051 is a Harvard-architecture 8-bit microcontroller: code space, data space and the SFR map are separate, and most SFR addresses are fixed by the design.
Every 8051 port is a latch plus a driver, so a pin used as input must first be written 1, and read-modify-write instructions act on the latch, not the pin.
Timer/counter blocks count machine cycles or falling edges on T0/T1, and TMOD picks one of four modes, with mode 1 (16-bit) the usual choice for delays.
The UART sends and receives bytes through the two halves of SBUF, Timer 1 supplies the baud clock, and RS-232 needs a MAX232-style level converter.
Five sources share two external pins, two timers and one serial port; each has a fixed vector, IE enables it, IP prioritises it, and flags clear by hardware or software depending on the source.
Embedded C keeps C syntax but adds SFR declarations, bit variables, volatile data and memory models so that code and data fit the small address space.
PIC18F452 and MSP430 differ from the 8051 and from each other: PIC uses 16-bit instructions with banked 8-bit data, while MSP430 uses a 16-bit RISC core built for low power.
Almost every long answer on this unit is a small program: pick the SFR settings, compute the count or baud value, then write the loop or ISR.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are scored on a labelled block diagram or SFR bit table, a step-by-step count or baud calculation with units, and a short assembly or C program whose SFR settings can be traced line by line.

bank.q: Draw the functional block diagram of the 8051 and explain each block: CPU, program memory, data memory, SFRs, ports, timers, serial port and interrupt unit.
outline: CPU is 8-bit with A, B, PSW, SP, PC and DPTR registers
4 KB on-chip program memory, 128 bytes internal RAM, up to 64 KB external code and data
SFR map 80H–FFH controls ports, timers, UART and interrupts
Four 8-bit ports, two 16-bit timer/counters, full-duplex UART
Five interrupt sources with fixed vectors
Harvard split: code and data have separate spaces and buses

bank.q: Explain the internal memory organization of the 8051, including register banks, the bit-addressable area, SFR space and external memory access.
outline: 128 bytes RAM: bank 0–3 at 00H–1FH selected by RS1,RS0
Bit-addressable area 20H–2FH, 16 bytes = 128 bits
Scratch pad 30H–7FH used as stack and variables
SFR space 80H–FFH, only bit-addressable addresses 80H,88H,...,F8H
Stack grows upward from the value in SP; SP resets to 07H
EA=1 uses internal code memory up to 4 KB, then external; EA=0 all external
PSEN for code fetch, RD and WR for external data

bank.q: Describe the 40-pin pin functions of the 8051, grouping pins by function.
outline: Port 0 (39–32): AD0–AD7 multiplexed address/data, needs external pull-ups
Port 1 (1–8): general purpose, also T2 in 8052
Port 2 (21–28): A8–A15 high address byte in external memory
Port 3 (10–17): INT0, INT1, T0, T1, WR, RD, TXD, RXD alternate functions
PSEN, ALE, EA, RST, XTAL1, XTAL2, Vcc, GND
RST is active high; two machine cycles needed for reset

bank.q: Explain the TMOD register bit by bit and describe the four timer modes of the 8051.
outline: TMOD at 89H: GATE, C/T, M1, M0 for timer 1 in high nibble and timer 0 in low nibble
Mode 0: 13-bit, THx 8 bits + TLx 5 bits
Mode 1: 16-bit, max count 65536
Mode 2: 8-bit auto-reload, TLx counts and THx reloads
Mode 3: timer 0 splits into two 8-bit timers; timer 1 stops (used only for baud rate)
GATE=1 makes INTx pin gate the run; C/T=1 counts T0/T1 falling edges

bank.q: Explain the 8051 interrupt structure: sources, vector addresses, IE and IP registers, and the flag-clearing rule for each source.
outline: Five sources: INT0, Timer 0, INT1, Timer 1, serial
Vector addresses 0003H, 000BH, 0013H, 001BH, 0023H with the main program above 0030H
IE bits EA, ES, ET1, EX1, ET0, EX0; EA is the master switch
IP gives two levels; a high-priority source can interrupt a low-priority ISR
TF0/TF1 and IE0/IE1 (edge) cleared by hardware on entry; IE0/IE1 (level) follows the pin
TI and RI must be cleared by software in the ISR, else the interrupt repeats

bank.q: Using a 12 MHz crystal, write assembly language and C programs to generate a 50 ms delay with Timer 0 in mode 1. Show the count calculation.
outline: Machine cycle = 12/12 MHz = 1 µs
50 ms needs 50,000 machine cycles
TMOD = 01H; set TR0 = 1, wait for TF0 = 1, clear TF0
Assembly: MOV TMOD,#01H; MOV TH0,#3CH; MOV TL0,#0B0H; SETB TR0; JNB TF0,$; CLR TF0
C: TMOD=0x01; TH0=0x3C; TL0=0xB0; TR0=1; while(!TF0); TF0=0;
For longer delays repeat the loop and count with a register

bank.q: With an 11.0592 MHz crystal, write a program to transmit the character 'A' and receive one character serially at 9600 baud in mode 1. Show the TH1 value.
outline: Oscillator 11.0592 MHz chosen so the baud rate divides exactly
SCON = 50H for 8-bit UART, REN = 1 to receive; TMOD high nibble = 20H for Timer 1 mode 2
Start Timer 1 with TR1 = 1
Transmit: MOV SBUF,#'A'; JNB TI,$; CLR TI
Receive: JNB RI,$; MOV A,SBUF; CLR RI
Mode 1 frame: 1 start bit, 8 data bits LSB first, 1 stop bit = 10 bits

bank.q: Eight LEDs are connected to port 1 and eight switches to port 2. Write a program that copies the switch pattern to the LEDs and explain why 0FFH must be written to port 2 first.
outline: MOV P2,#0FFH makes each port 2 pin an input by turning off the strong pull-down
Loop: MOV A,P2 reads the pin state
MOV P1,A drives the LEDs; a 0 sinks current and lights the LED
Explain latch versus pin: writing 1 makes the pin float high and readable
No external pull-ups needed on ports 1–3 because of the internal weak pull-up
Add a small delay or debounce if switches are mechanical

bank.q: Configure Timer 0 as a counter in mode 1 to count pulses applied to the T0 pin and display the low byte of the count on port 1. Explain each register setting.
outline: TMOD = 05H: C/T = 1 for counter, M1M0 = 01 for 16-bit
TL0 counts falling edges on T0 (P3.4); TH0 counts TL0 overflows
Start with TR0 = 1; read TH0 and TL0 for the count
MOV P1,TL0 displays the low byte
Maximum count 65536 before TF0 sets; clear TF0 in software
A counter needs a minimum pulse width and one machine cycle to detect an edge

bank.q: Write embedded C for the 8051 that toggles an LED on port 1.0 in an external interrupt 0 service routine. Explain whether edge or level triggering should be chosen and how the flag behaves.
outline: Declare sbit LED = P1^0; and use the interrupt keyword with vector 0
IT0 = 1 selects falling-edge triggering on INT0
EX0 = 1, EA = 1 enable the source
ISR must be short: toggle the bit, no long delay inside
Edge-triggered flag IE0 is cleared by hardware on entry; level-triggered follows the pin and clears when the pin goes high
Declare shared variables volatile if changed inside the ISR

bank.q: Write a C program that receives bytes on the serial port using the serial interrupt and copies each received byte to port 1. Explain how RI is cleared and why the ISR must read SBUF.
outline: SCON = 50H; TMOD = 20H; TH1 = 0FDH; TR1 = 1 for 9600 baud at 11.0592 MHz
ES = 1 and EA = 1 enable the serial interrupt
ISR checks RI, reads SBUF into a variable, writes it to P1, then clears RI
Reading SBUF is what fetches the received byte; not reading it loses data
Clearing RI inside the ISR prevents the same interrupt retriggering forever
Vector 0023H is shared by transmit and receive; test TI and RI separately

bank.q: Compare a microprocessor and a microcontroller on architecture, memory, I/O, instruction set and application, and justify which one suits a washing-machine controller.
outline: Microprocessor: CPU only, external RAM/ROM and I/O, general-purpose instruction set, high speed, high power
Microcontroller: CPU plus memory, timers, serial port and I/O on one chip, bit-manipulation instructions, low cost and power
List comparison table covering pins, clock, addressing, interrupts
Washing machine needs few inputs, timer delays, motor and valve outputs, cost and reliability matter
A microcontroller such as the 8051 removes external glue logic and is the right choice

bank.q: A design needs a 1 s delay from an 8051 running at 12 MHz. Evaluate timer modes 1 and 2 for this job and calculate the reload values, including the error from crystal tolerance.
outline: Machine cycle 1 µs, so 1 s = 1,000,000 counts, beyond 65536
Mode 1: repeat 50 ms blocks 20 times, or use a nested software count
Mode 2 auto-reload is convenient only for short fixed periods up to 256 counts
Show the reload arithmetic and the number of repetitions
Crystal tolerance of a common crystal, roughly tens of ppm, gives timing error growing with delay
Better: use an interrupt-driven block so the CPU is free, or use a hardware real-time clock

bank.q: Compare the 8051, PIC18F452 and MSP430 on architecture, data width, instruction width, memory banking and power, and choose one for a battery-powered sensor node that wakes once a minute.
outline: 8051: 8-bit, Harvard, variable-length instructions, 128 bytes RAM, four register banks, no low-power modes
PIC18F452: 8-bit data, 16-bit instructions, banked data memory selected by BSR, 2 KB RAM, 32 KB flash, many peripherals
MSP430: 16-bit RISC, orthogonal registers, seven addressing modes, LPM0–LPM4 with fast wake on interrupt
Sensor node: long sleep, short active time, so sleep current dominates the energy budget
MSP430 wins on sleep current and 16-bit arithmetic; 8051 wins on cost and familiarity
PIC sits in between with rich peripherals and wide tool support

bank.q: Explain why an RS-232 link needs a MAX232 between the 8051 and a PC, describe the connections, and evaluate the limits of the arrangement.
outline: 8051 TXD gives TTL 0 V and 5 V; RS-232 uses about +3 V to +15 V for 0 and −3 V to −15 V for 1, inverted logic
MAX232 charge pumps make the required positive and negative rails from a single 5 V supply
TXD (P3.1) to T1IN, R1OUT to RXD (P3.0), T1OUT and R1IN to the DB9
Common ground, RTS/CTS optional; use the correct baud rate, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit
Limits: short cable length, modest baud rate, point-to-point only, no addressing or multi-drop
For a board-to-board link inside a product, plain TTL or RS-485 is usually preferred

glossary.def: A single chip containing a CPU, memory, timers, and I/O peripherals for embedded control.
Time of one clock cycle fed to XTAL1 and XTAL2; the machine cycle is 12 such periods in the standard 8051.
16-bit register holding the address of the next instruction byte to fetch.
8-bit register at the centre of arithmetic, logic and data movement instructions.
One of four groups of eight registers at 00H–1FH, selected by bits RS1 and RS0 in PSW.
Bytes 20H–2FH whose 128 bits can each be set, cleared and tested by single instructions.
8-bit SFR at 81H that holds the address of the last byte pushed; the 8051 stack lives in internal RAM.
The flip-flop behind each port pin that stores the value the program wrote.
Current a pin accepts when pulled low and delivers when pulled high; 8051 pins sink much more than they source.
Bit set by hardware when the timer counter rolls over from all 1s to 0.
Mode 2 behaviour where the low byte counts and the high byte reloads it on every overflow.
A divider placed before a counter so the counter sees a slower clock; the 8051 timer input is already divided by 12.
One-way, either-direction-in-turn, and both-directions-at-once data flow; the 8051 UART is full-duplex.
Framing bits in an asynchronous frame: a 0 starts the frame and a 1 ends it.
Bit 7 of PCON at 87H; SMOD=1 doubles the serial baud rate in modes 1, 2 and 3.
Code placed at a vector address that runs in response to an interrupt and ends with RETI.
Return-from-interrupt instruction that restores the PC and re-enables lower-priority interrupts.
Time from the flag being set to the first instruction of the ISR running; it includes finishing the current instruction.
Testing a flag repeatedly in software instead of using the interrupt mechanism.
Special Function Register: a memory-mapped control register in the 80H–FFH address range.
A compiler that runs on a PC but produces machine code for the microcontroller.
Compiler option (small, compact, large) that fixes where variables are placed in the 8051 address space.
Driving a protocol in software by toggling port pins, with no dedicated peripheral.
A counter that resets the CPU if software fails to clear it within a set time.
Hardware that runs and traces the microcontroller's program inside a real circuit for debugging.
